newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-Mayors in crossfire of Colombia's guerrilla war.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mayors in crossfire of Colombia's guerrilla war.

text.p: Dodamin Trujillo's toughest job as mayor of Caldono was helping to remove the bodies of two local officials who had been shot and dumped in a ravine on the outskirts of his town in southwest Colombia.

A week later, the 35-year-old mayor was in hiding. After weathering two attacks by leftist guerrillas and countless death threats since his 1994 election, he fled in early July along the mud roads that wind out of the jagged river valley where Caldono nestles in the mountains of Cauca province.

"When I die I want it to be in that little village, but not when a gang of killers decides," Trujillo told Reuters by telephone from an undisclosed location outside Cauca. "They don't deserve the pleasure of murdering me."

Small-town mayors like Trujillo, a political independent, have stepped increasingly into the crossfire of armed groups competing for political control of the countryside. Government officials accuse leftist rebels, mainly the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and the National Liberation Army (ELN), of assassinating and kidnapping civic leaders in a bid to impose regional control.
Human rights organisations say right-wing paramilitary groups use similar tactics with the military's tacit support.
At least 19 mayors have been assassinated and more kidnapped by armed political groups since January 1996, according to the Colombian Federation of Municipalities. Five mayors were murdered in 1995.

Colombia is bracing for an upswing in political bloodshed when the campaign season for October elections officially begins this month since leftist rebels and right-wing death squads alike have vowed to prevent candidates they oppose from campaigning.

"There is great worry about the upcoming elections," said Hector Henao, who directs a human rights office for the National Council of Bishops. "Elections often mean violence here and everything we see shows it's getting worse."
For Trujillo, who is ineligible for reelection, political violence is more than a campaign season problem.

"Violence comes from all sides and poisons the environment," he told Reuters in Caldono three weeks before he went into hiding. "The state is not in control here and anyone who wants to kill can kill."

With its tree-lined central plaza and whitewashed Spanish church, Caldono might figure in a tourist guide of colonial- style Colombian villages. But the civic buildings near the central plaza are pocked with bullet holes and the parish priest fled in June after receiving death threats.
THREE ATTACKS AROUND THE TOWN THIS YEAR

The town is the centre of a municipality of just 20,000 farmers, about half of whom are members of the Paez Indian community, who tend small plots in a lush but steep valley that is shrouded in the morning by a thick fog. The FARC's highly active Sixth Front has flexed its muscle three times this year within 20 miles (32 km) of Caldono, attacking police installations in the town and neighbouring villages.

Colombian soldiers, who have been in Caldono since a FARC attack in February that flattened the municipal schoolhouse where the national police had taken up residence, fill restaurants and lounge amidst the rubble left by the fighting.

Trujillo said he still did not know who delivered the threats to his little office near the central square, only that they began on his first day in office and continued until the morning gunmen dragged Caldono's town council president and a public works inspector from their homes and shot them execution style.

"We can't be sure -- it could be the guerrillas, paramilitaries or just some political rival," Trujillo said. "Someone hiding in the darkness has yet to be sated by the blood that has already been spilled."
